title: Physiology, Synuclein -- Introduction
content: Synucleins are soluble proteins found primarily in nervous system tissue and in specific tumors. There are 3 families of synuclein: alpha-synuclein, beta-synuclein, and gamma-synuclein. The alpha and beta variants are found in presynaptic terminals, whereas the gamma variant is expressed in the peripheral nervous system and retina. The gamma variant is also expressed in breast tumors and serves as a marker for disease progression. Alpha-synuclein is the most studied variant due to its association with Parkinson disease and is the focus of this topic. Alpha-synuclein is the product of the SNCA gene. It is a small protein that is expressed in neurons near synaptic vesicles at presynaptic terminals. Recent studies have shown that alpha-synuclein is involved in synaptic vesicle recycling, but the exact mechanism remains unclear. The protein becomes pathologic when it aggregates and leads to neuron dysfunction, then subsequent cell death. [1] [2] [3] [4]

title: Physiology, Synuclein -- Issues of Concern
content: Synucleins are proteins of interest due to their involvement in synucleinopathies. Synucleinopathies include Parkinson disease, dementia with Lewy Bodies, and multiple system atrophy. Alpha-synuclein is strongly linked to Parkinson disease (see Image. Alpha-Synucleins Aggregated and Folded in the Brain Area). Research shows that alpha-synuclein accumulation impairs lysosomal autophagy. Additionally, mutations in alpha-synuclein lead to the generation of aberrant proteins, which further impair lysosomal proteolytic pathways and result in neuronal cell death. [5] Beta-synuclein is generally neuroprotective as it can inhibit alpha-synuclein aggregation, but in specific cases, it can be pathologic. Rare cases of dementia with Lewy bodies have been found with point mutations in beta-synuclein, leading to a neurotoxic effect. [6]

title: Physiology, Synuclein -- Issues of Concern
content: Multiple system atrophy characteristically demonstrates autonomic failure, Parkinsonism, and ataxia. It is a sporadic, adult-onset, progressive disorder. The pathologic hallmark presentation of multiple system atrophy is glial cytoplasmic inclusions of misfolded alpha-synuclein, found in oligodendrocytes. Multiple system atrophy predominantly affects the striatonigral and olivopontocerebellar structures. Multiple system atrophy has 2 main motor phenotypes, Parkinsonian and cerebellar. Clinical differentiation from Parkinson disease is not possible and requires neuropathology for definitive diagnosis. [7] [8] In animal models, research has shown that the absence of gamma-synuclein in the central nervous system reduces the ability to use information (memory) to manage and solve tasks and problems. Still, in the animal model, gamma-synuclein has been shown to recruit macrophages to the site of optic nerve damage and to stimulate scar tissue formation. In both animal studies mentioned above, elderly mice showed a reduction in the expression of this protein.

title: Physiology, Synuclein -- Cellular Level
content: The SNCA gene encodes synuclein, a protein composed of 140 amino acids. The resulting amino acid sequence can, via prolonged incubation, code for alpha-helices by binding to negatively charged lipids or for beta-sheets. The protein is made up of 3 regions: an amino terminus, central hydrophobic, and a carboxyl terminus. The amino-terminal regions adopt alpha-helical conformations and contain apolipoprotein lipid-binding motifs. The central hydrophobic regions can promote beta-sheet formation. Lastly, the carboxyl terminus is generally unstructured. [6]

title: Physiology, Synuclein -- Cellular Level
content: Alpha-synuclein is present in living structures in a perpetual balance between the soluble state and a state in which it links to the membrane. Membrane bonding occurs thanks to the presence of phosphatidylinositol or phosphatidylserine; at the brain level, the protein binds to small vesicles (about 40 nm in diameter). Alpha-synuclein can form multiple polymorphic aggregates, collectively referred to as strains. This aggregation capacity is most likely a reason for the different types of synucleinopathies observed; each strain recruits other proteins differently, thereby creating distinct dysfunctional patterns. Beta-synuclein is made up of 134 amino acids, while gamma-synuclein is made up of 127 amino acids, which bind membrane phospholipids.

title: Physiology, Synuclein -- Development
content: Alpha-synuclein expression inducement occurs during neuronal development. It occurs after neuronal differentiation and the formation of synaptic connections. Additionally, alpha-synuclein levels fluctuate in conditions that alter neuroplasticity or result in neural injury. [6] In the human model, alpha-synuclein is present in the fetus since the fifteenth week of gestation; during the fetal period, the protein is present in all organs.

title: Physiology, Synuclein -- Organ Systems Involved
content: Alpha-synuclein is predominantly found in the nervous system, composing 1% of total cytosolic protein. Alpha-synuclein is also abundant in erythrocytes and platelets, although for reasons unknown. [6] Functional alteration of this protein causes anemia and incomplete maturation of the red cells. Alpha-synuclein is also present in the cerebrospinal fluid of patients with Parkinson disease and healthy subjects. This protein is mainly expressed in the brain and is found in specific brain areas at higher levels (such as the beta form): the cerebellum, hippocampus, neocortex, thalamus, and striatum. Alpha-synuclein is present at low levels in other tissues, including muscle, kidney, motor neurons, liver, heart, and lungs, as well as in the olfactory epithelium, lymphocytes, and testes. Gamma-synuclein is found mainly in the peripheral nervous system, the sympathetic system, and the brain.

title: Physiology, Synuclein -- Function
content: Alpha-synuclein plays several roles in synaptic firing, as determined by experiments over the past decade. It can alter neurotransmitter release, is involved with vesicular trafficking, and works with cysteine string protein-alpha as a chaperone protein in the assembly of soluble N-ethylmaleimide-sensitive factor attachment protein receptor (SNARE) complexes. In experiments on bovine neural tissue, beta-synuclein has functioned as a constitutive inhibitor of phospholipase D2. Phospholipase D2 is involved in cytoskeleton reorganization and endocytosis at the plasma membrane. Researchers have also suggested beta-synuclein to be a natural negative regulator of alpha-synuclein aggregation, leading to anti-amyloidogenic properties. Lastly, gamma-synuclein was identified as a marker for breast cancer via cDNA sequencing. The cellular function of gamma-synuclein is unknown. [1] [6] [9] [10] [11] [12]

title: Physiology, Synuclein -- Function
content: The alpha-synuclein protein was first identified in the electric organ of the stingray Torpedo californica in 1988, in the presynaptic area and at the nuclear envelope. From these areas derives the protein's name: synaptic vesicles ("syn") and nuclear envelope ("nuclein"). Although decades have passed since its discovery, its functions remain not fully elucidated, especially in a physiological environment. Beta-synuclein protein was identified in 2 animal model studies (1990 and 1992) in the brain, at the presynaptic level of nerve endings. Gamma-synuclein was identified in breast cancer in 1997.

title: Physiology, Synuclein -- Mechanism
content: Researchers have identified several pathogenic mechanisms of synucleins, but the mechanisms underlying normal cellular function remain unclear. Presynaptic nerve terminals function via the repeated release of neurotransmitters and, as such, require constant cycling of the SNARE complex. Experiments have shown that alpha-synuclein plays a nonclassical chaperone role in maintaining presynaptic SNARE complex assembly. Alpha-synuclein can be found bound to the SNARE protein synaptobrevin-2/vesicle-associated membrane protein 2. This interaction maintains the SNARE complex in an assembled state and prevents the presynaptic nerve terminal from releasing neurotransmitters. [13]

title: Physiology, Synuclein -- Mechanism
content: Alpha-synuclein undergoes several posttranslational changes, particularly in its carboxy-terminal tail portion: ubiquitination; sumoylation (stimulates protein solubility); glycation; glycosylation; nitration (inhibits the binding to lipid vesicles); proteolysis; phosphorylation (inhibits its aggregation); oxidation; acetylation (increases its shape and helical folding, with aggregation resistance and greater affinity with membrane bonds). These adaptations lead to the construction of new structures and to changes in binding affinity.

title: Physiology, Synuclein -- Related Testing
content: One of the hallmarks of Parkinson disease is alpha-synuclein-containing Lewy body inclusions in the substantia nigra. Parkinson disease is a clinical diagnosis, but eosinophilic inclusions of alpha-synuclein as Lewy bodies are definitive. [14] [15] Additionally, experimentation is underway to find a peripheral biomarker to identify Parkinson disease in patients. Real-time quaking-induced conversion assay functions by vigorous shaking and agitation to induce fibril formation of proteins. Research has revealed that biopsied submandibular gland tissue can be tested via real-time quaking-induced conversion assays for Parkinson disease with high specificity and sensitivity via pathological alpha-synuclein. [16] [17]

title: Physiology, Synuclein -- Pathophysiology
content: Parkinson disease hallmarks include dopaminergic neuron loss in the substantia nigra pars compacta and Lewy bodies. The exact mechanism of Parkinson disease is unknown, but it involves alpha-synuclein aggregates, the endo-lysosomal system, and mitochondrial function. Alpha-synuclein is a presynaptic protein that assists in presynaptic vesicle transportation and endocytosis. When misfolded and aggregated, it becomes toxic to mitochondria and neurons. Increased cellular oxidative stress promotes alpha-synuclein aggregation. As alpha-synuclein aggregates, mitochondria, and the neuron's lysosomal function deteriorate, the cell eventually dies. [15] Alpha-synuclein is also involved in other pathologies, such as the Lewy body variant of Alzheimer disease, multiple system atrophy, and brain neurodegeneration with an accumulation of iron (accumulation type I).

title: Physiology, Synuclein -- Clinical Significance
content: Synuclein is clinically significant because of its central role in synucleinopathies, including Parkinson disease, dementia with Lewy bodies, and multiple system atrophy. Alpha-synuclein is the target of much research and could serve as a target for therapeutic agents. Suggested therapies include targeting alpha-synuclein aggregates with specific antibodies to promote clearance, targeting alpha-synuclein monomers to increase clearance, decrease synthesis, or stabilize the monomers to prevent aggregation. [18]

title: Physiology, Synuclein -- Clinical Significance
content: Beta-synuclein is an intrinsically disordered protein but has been shown to inhibit alpha-synuclein aggregation, with implications for synucleinopathies. The 3 synuclein domains of beta-synuclein have been demonstrated to inhibit the aggregation of alpha-synuclein. This fact is of clinical significance, as interactions among synuclein chains can serve as a basis for targeted therapeutics against alpha-synuclein aggregates. [19]

title: Physiology, Synuclein -- Clinical Significance
content: Synuclein-gamma has implications in various types of cancers. For breast cancer, radiation therapy following mastectomy reduces recurrence and improves prognosis. Yet, radiotherapy comes with a litany of side effects and risks. Patients who were positive for synuclein-gamma showed a poorer response to radiation therapy, possibly due to a correlation between gamma-synuclein and expression of radiation repair genes. [20]
